Lesson 3.2 · 20 min · Verified 17 Jul 2026

Credit policy as data: eligibility and the decision engine

After this lesson you can:
  • Explain FOIR and the standard eligibility knockouts
  • Describe why policy lives as versioned data, not code
  • State the decision engine's guarantees: deterministic, fail-closed, replayable
On this page
  1. What a credit policy actually says
  2. Policy is data, versioned and approved
  3. The engine that says no by default
  4. Where this lives in LoanOS
  5. Knowledge check

1. What a credit policy actually says

Strip the mystique and a retail credit policy is a structured document: who may borrow (age band, residency, occupation classes), how much (amount and tenor bounds, exposure caps), affordability (FOIR — the share of income already committed to obligations plus the new EMI, capped by policy, e.g. 'total obligations may not exceed 55% of verified income'), knockouts (minimum bureau score, no recent write-offs, no active fraud flags), and pricing (rate grids by risk grade, fees, penal-charge policy).

Deviations happen — a good customer just above the FOIR cap — and are themselves governed: a deviation matrix defines who may approve which departure, at which level.

2. Policy is data, versioned and approved

LoanOS's rule is that lending policy never lives as scattered if-statements in application code. A policy is a decision model: a JSON artefact with effective dates, validated against a golden corpus of test cases, approved four-eyes, signed and bound to a tenant. Changing policy means shipping a new version with evidence — not editing production behaviour in place.

For a BA this is liberating: 'change the FOIR cap to 50% for salaried applicants from 1 August' is a policy-version change request with a test corpus, an approval trail and an effective date — a fully specifiable, fully auditable artefact.

3. The engine that says no by default

Policies are evaluated by the per-tenant decision engine — deliberately boring in the best way:

  • Deterministic — no clock, no randomness, no network in evaluation; the same inputs always produce the same answer.
  • Exact — money math uses exact decimals; floats are forbidden on the evaluation path.
  • Fail-closed — missing facts, expired policy, unreachable service: the outcome is refer or deny, never approve.
  • Replayable — every decision's audit record lets you re-run it byte-identically years later.

Outcomes are approve, refer or deny with reason codes. 'Refer' is not an error: it is the engine handing a case to human judgement, which module 7 picks up.

Regulatory anchors

  • RBI-IT-GRC — Straight-through-processing controls and audit trails demand exactly this discipline around automated decisions.
  • RBI-DL-2025 — Credit assessment must be demonstrably the RE's own act — versioned policy with lineage proves it.

Family IDs resolve in the India regulatory register (docs/compliance/india-regulatory-register.md), which owns sources and caveats.

Where this lives in LoanOS

  • Capability UWG-009 — EMI, FOIR, age, amount and tenor eligibility.
  • Capability UWG-018 — Deterministic decision models with golden corpus.
  • Capability UWG-019 — Decision trace, policy/data/model lineage and replay.
  • Document docs/architecture/decision-engine-design.md — Engine source of truth: invariants INV-1 (determinism), INV-5 (fail closed), INV-6 (exact money).
  • Code rules/ — The Rust decision-engine workspace — one isolated runtime per tenant.
  • Operating guide configure-product (open in the Guide) — Operating guide: configure a lending product as effective-dated policy.

Key terms

FOIR Decision engine Policy bundle EMI

Knowledge check

1. A borrower earns ₹1,00,000/month, pays ₹30,000 in existing EMIs, and the new loan's EMI is ₹18,000. Policy caps FOIR at 45%. What happens?

  1. Approved — 30% is under the cap
  2. Referred or declined — total FOIR is 48%, over the cap
  3. Approved — new EMI alone is under 45%
  4. FOIR doesn't apply to salaried borrowers
Show answer

B. FOIR counts total fixed obligations: (30,000 + 18,000) / 1,00,000 = 48% > 45%. The policy outcome is the restrictive one, possibly with a governed deviation path.

2. Why does the decision engine read no clock and no network during evaluation?

  1. Performance
  2. So every decision is deterministic and byte-replayable from its audit record
  3. Cost savings
  4. Security theatre
Show answer

B. Determinism is the foundation of replay: an auditor must be able to reproduce any historical decision exactly from recorded inputs and the policy version.
